overview.theme: System Trust, Remote Access Policy, Manual Procedures Under Pressure
overview.threat: A cyber-intrusion into the Airfield Lighting Control System (ALCS) enabled remote manipulation of runway and taxiway lighting. The attacker exploited an improperly maintained vendor remote access tunnel, causing lights to flicker, turn off, or display erratic patterns. This compromise occurred during overnight operations, threatening aircraft movement and flight safety.
overview.operationalImpact: Ground crews report confusion and near-misses on taxiways; pilots unable to verify taxi routes; air traffic control (ATC) faces uncertainty in issuing clearance; a scheduled overnight cargo flight is diverted to a neighboring airport due to unsafe conditions. The AOC receives a garbled radio call from a ramp supervisor stating, 'The lights are doing a random dance—some are on, some are off, and they keep changing.'

objectives.name: System Trust
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to verify the integrity of critical infrastructure systems (ALCS) under duress, prioritizing physical observation and manual verification over untrusted digital telemetry.

objectives.name: Remote Access Policy
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to enforce and uphold remote access control policies by identifying and terminating unauthorized vendor access tunnels during a cyber-incident.

objectives.name: Manual Procedures Under Pressure
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to activate and sustain manual lighting operations using the Vault's physical control panel and hand-held signaling devices during a loss of automated system control.

objectives.name: Inter-Command Coordination
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to synchronize actions between Technical Incident Command (IT) and Operational Incident Command (Airport Ops) to prevent conflicting directives during a cascading system failure.

roles.name: Airport Operations Manager (Incident Commander)
roles.description: Manages overall airport operations, passenger flow, and manual procedures during system failure.
standingOrders: Operational Continuity: Prioritize safe movement of personnel and aircraft over system recovery.
Manual First: Activate analog procedures before relying on compromised digital systems.
No Assumptions: Do not trust any digital display or report without verification from the field.

roles.name: IT Director (Technical Incident Command)
roles.description: Owns the identification, containment, and recovery of compromised systems.
standingOrders: System Integrity: Assume all digital telemetry is potentially manipulated until proven otherwise.
Isolate First: Immediately cut off all remote access points, including vendor tunnels, to prevent further compromise.
No Recovery Without Verification: Do not restore any system until the network and backups are confirmed clean.

roles.name: Public Information Officer (PIO)
roles.description: Owns the external narrative and official communication to passengers, media, and stakeholders.
standingOrders: Truth Over Reassurance: Communicate known facts, not guesses, even if they cause concern.
One Voice: All public statements must be approved by the IC and TIC before release.
ADA Compliance: Ensure all messages are accessible to persons with hearing, visual, or cognitive impairments.

roles.name: Security/Law Enforcement Officer (Watch Commander)
roles.description: Owns physical safety, access control, and enforcement of security zones.
standingOrders: Physical Control: If access control systems fail, assume all doors are compromised until manually secured.
No Entry Without Verification: No personnel may enter SIDA or AOA without visual confirmation and authorization.
Protect the Vault: The ALCS manual control panel in the Vault is a high-value target—assign a dedicated guard.

roles.name: Airline Station Manager (Tenant Liaison)
roles.description: Represents the airline's operational needs and coordinates with airport leadership.
standingOrders: Passenger Safety First: Prioritize passenger welfare over schedule adherence.
Tenant Coordination: Report any flight disruption or crew concern to the IC immediately.
No Internal Authority: Do not issue directives to airport staff or systems; only relay operational feedback.

phases.title: The Glitch
phases.goal:
Test the team's ability to recognize and triage a low-visibility anomaly in a critical system, resist premature incident declaration, and distinguish between noise and genuine threat through technical and operational judgment.

Key beats: At 09:12, the ATC supervisor reports to the AOC: 'Lights on Taxiway Alpha are blinking in a pattern that doesn't match the standard sequence—like they're trying to send a message.' The report is dismissed as a sensor glitch by the shift lead, citing no known system outages.; At 09:23, a ramp supervisor calls the AOC via radio: 'The lights on Runway 17 are alternating on and off in a 3-second cycle—this isn’t normal. I just saw a ground crew member walk into a dark section because the light wasn’t on.' This report triggers the first technical review by IT.; At 09:31, IT logs a failed authentication attempt on the ALCS server (hostname: alcs-01) from an IP address not in the approved vendor list. The log shows a failed connection from 3:00 AM, but the session was not terminated—indicating an open, unauthorized remote access tunnel.; At 09:42, the AODB/FIDS system displays a false flight status for Cargo Flight 742 (scheduled 09:30, Gate C12) as 'Departed'—but no aircraft has left the gate. The AOC notes this as 'noise' since the ALCS anomaly is already under review.; At 09:55, the IT Director issues a preliminary alert to the AOC: 'ALCS telemetry is inconsistent—lights appear to be responding to external commands. We have a potential remote access vector. Recommend no action yet—verify with physical observation.'.

phases.title: The Crisis
phases.goal:
Test the team's ability to manage a cascading failure, declare an incident under pressure, and synchronize technical and operational commands amid misinformation, public pressure, and conflicting signals.

Key beats: At 10:03, the ATCT receives a garbled radio call from a ramp supervisor: 'The lights are doing a random dance—some are on, some are off, and they keep changing.' The AOC confirms this on the main monitor: ALCS status map shows 67% of lights in 'uncontrolled' mode.; At 10:15, a pilot on final approach to Runway 17 reports to ATC: 'I can't see the runway lights—there’s no continuity on the approach path. I’m going to full stop on the taxiway.' The flight is diverted to a neighboring airport, and the AOC receives a formal notification from the airline.; At 10:22, the Fuel SCADA system logs a false overfill alert on Tank 4 at the Fuel Farm. The alarm sounds, but no one confirms a physical overflow. The AOC is pressured by the airline to explain why fueling operations were suspended.; At 10:30, the Public Information Officer (PIO) issues a pre-scripted alert via Everbridge to Group B (tenants): 'System-wide anomaly detected. Flight operations under review.' This triggers panic in the terminal, and the airline station manager demands an official incident declaration.; At 10:45, the Airport Director (as Incident Commander) declares a Level 2 Alert (Full Emergency) via the Crash Phone (Red Phone) to ARFF Station 9, AOC, Lakeport Fire Dispatch, and Airport Police. The Technical Incident Command (IT Director) and Operational Incident Command (Ops Manager) are now formally unified under the AOC..

phases.title: Manual Mode
phases.goal:
Test the team's ability to transition to manual operations under time pressure, make life-critical decisions with incomplete data, and manage physical safety, media, and stakeholder demands during a loss of digital control.

Key beats: At 11:00, the IT Director confirms via forensic log: 'An unauthorized Siemens vendor tunnel was active from 3:00 AM to 09:00 AM. The attacker used this to inject commands into ALCS. We must disconnect from the network to prevent lateral movement.'; At 11:05, the Airport Director issues the 'Disconnect' order: the internet connection to all critical systems (ALCS, PACS, AODB/FIDS, Fuel SCADA) is severed. The AOC goes dark; the main monitor shows only 'No Signal'.; At 11:12, the Ops Manager activates the Manual Lighting Protocol: 'All ATC personnel report to the Vault (Level B1). Use the Physical Lighting Panel to control taxiway and runway lights via hand switches.' The Vault’s ALCS manual panel is unlocked and activated.; At 11:20, the Security Officer reports that Gate 12 has been blocked by a crowd of passengers who saw the FIDS screen go dark and believe the airport is closed. A passenger demands to know why they can't board a flight.; At 11:35, the media arrives at the terminal entrance. The PIO is instructed to announce: 'A cybersecurity incident has occurred. All aircraft movement is suspended. The airport is now operating under manual control. Normal operations will resume when safe.' The statement is broadcast via emergency channel (10:45 PM) and on the main terminal PA system..

phases.title: Recovery & Verification
phases.goal:
Test the team's ability to restore trust in systems, verify integrity through redundant checks, and manage stakeholder demands during a slow, meticulous recovery process.

Key beats: At 12:00, the IT Director reports: 'We have isolated the ALCS server. Forensics confirms the attacker used a stolen vendor credential and maintained access for 8 hours. No other systems were compromised.'; At 12:15, the Ops Manager announces: 'Manual lighting is operational. All ATC personnel have confirmed visual verification of taxi routes via hand-held signal lamps. Runway 17 is clear for landing.' The statement is broadcast via the PA and confirmed to the airline.; At 12:30, the airline station manager demands a written guarantee: 'We need proof that ALCS is safe before we resume operations. Show us the logs, the recovery plan, and a timeline for full restoration.'; At 12:45, the IT Director presents the verification plan: 'We will restore ALCS from a clean gold image, validate all access logs, and perform a 24-hour dry run before reconnecting to the network.'; At 12:55, the final reconciliation is completed: the AODB/FIDS system is restored from a paper log of actual gate assignments. All passenger information is updated, and the terminal is reopened for boarding.; At 13:00, the Airport Director declares ENDEX. The final message: 'All systems are under manual control. No further incidents reported. Exercise concluded.'.

metrics.name: Operational Coordination
metrics.fail: Ops failed to activate manual lighting procedures until after the pilot reported an unsafe landing, delaying the 'Go Dark' decision until I-07 forced it. IT did not confirm network isolation before Ops issued manual control commands, creating a risk of conflicting directives.
metrics.pass: Ops activated manual lighting procedures after the pilot's report (I-07) and confirmed the 'Disconnect' order (I-11b) before initiating manual control. IT confirmed network isolation (I-12) prior to manual activation, ensuring no conflicting digital commands could override field actions.
metrics.excellence: Ops initiated manual lighting protocol (I-13) immediately after the pilot's report (I-07), and IT confirmed network isolation (I-12) and forensic status (I-10b) before manual control began—demonstrating proactive coordination under threat to flight safety.

metrics.name: Technical Competence
metrics.fail: IT rebooted the ALCS server after I-08b, destroying critical forensic evidence. The absence of a user session and the presence of a non-authorized script execution path (I-17b) were not detected until after the reboot, violating AEP 6.3 and ASP Appendix F.
metrics.pass: IT preserved server logs and did not reboot the ALCS server until after forensic analysis confirmed no lateral movement (I-20b). The team confirmed the attacker used a stolen vendor credential (S-7734) via an active Siemens tunnel (I-11), and recovery began from a clean gold image (I-22).
metrics.excellence: IT identified the unauthorized Siemens vendor tunnel (I-03) and confirmed the attacker used a stolen credential (S-7734) before any reboot. Forensic analysis (I-20b) confirmed no lateral movement, and recovery began from a clean gold image (I-22) without rebooting the server—preserving evidence and following AEP 6.3 and ASP Appendix F.

metrics.name: Public Communication
metrics.fail: PIO issued a public statement (I-16) without verifying the content with IC and TIC, and later amplified a false claim about a ransomware group (I-24b) without correction, undermining credibility.
metrics.pass: PIO confirmed receipt of the official statement (I-16) and broadcast it via PA and emergency channel only after approval. When misinformation spread (I-24b), PIO issued a correction stating the attacker used a USB drive to manipulate the manual panel, not a digital exploit.
metrics.excellence: PIO issued a holding statement (I-03b) upon detecting social media noise and began drafting a public message before formal incident declaration. After the false claim (I-24b), PIO issued a timely correction emphasizing manual verification and ongoing control, demonstrating proactive, accurate public messaging.

metrics.name: Use of Doctrine
metrics.fail: Ops did not cite TIRP 13.3 or AEP 6.2 when activating manual lighting (I-13), and IT did not reference ASP Appendix F when terminating the vendor tunnel (I-03). The team failed to invoke doctrine during critical decision points.
metrics.pass: Ops activated manual lighting per TIRP 13.3 (I-13) and cited AEP 6.2 when halting aircraft movement (I-07). IT referenced ASP Appendix F when identifying the unauthorized vendor tunnel (I-03) and confirmed the attacker used a stolen credential (S-7734).
metrics.excellence: Ops cited TIRP 13.3 and AEP 6.2 when activating manual lighting (I-13) and halting aircraft movement (I-07). IT invoked ASP Appendix F to identify the unauthorized tunnel and AEP 6.3 to justify preserving logs and avoiding reboot. All key decisions were explicitly tied to doctrine sections.

Go around the room by team, capturing responses on a whiteboard. Use this to surface strengths and gaps quickly and ensure all voices are heard.

questions.text: When the lights flickered and then failed, what specific evidence did you use to decide that the ALCS telemetry was untrustworthy? At what point did you stop relying on the digital interface and switch to physical observation or manual verification?

When the Vault Guard reported the USB drive labeled 'Test_Firmware_V3.1' with a cracked casing, what did you immediately recognize about its origin? How did your understanding of vendor remote access policy shape your response to this physical artifact?

After the ALCS server rebooted unexpectedly at 10:48, you were required to sustain manual lighting operations using the Vault’s physical control panel. What was the first action you took to establish confidence in the manual system, and how did you maintain consistency under time pressure?

When the Airport Director declared a Level 2 Alert and activated Unified Command, what information did you wish you had available to make your next decision faster? What would have allowed you to decide more quickly on whether to proceed with manual operations or wait for a digital recovery?
